notes: Sentence appeal for section 24A Immigration Act deception; court declined to assess asylum claim strength and upheld nine-month term following Kolawole.

enrichment.short_title: R v Kishietine: sentence for entry by deception with asylum claim
key_facts: Congolese appellant entered on a false passport, later claimed asylum in a false name and admitted section 24A deception.
She pleaded guilty and was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment in the Crown Court at Warwick.
She argued the sentence was too long given a genuine asylum claim, torture history and no prior convictions.
Section 31 was unavailable because she had not presented herself without delay at entry.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) sentence appeal by leave of the Single Judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; nine-month sentence held appropriate for section 24A deception despite asserted genuine asylum claim.
enrichment.ratio: Courts should not routinely assess asylum claim genuineness when sentencing section 24A offences; deterrence justifies firm sentences and section 31's direct-entry conditions were not met on these facts.
legal_issues: Whether sentence should reflect genuineness of an asylum claim where section 31 does not apply
Whether the court should assess Refugee Convention claim strength at sentencing
Appropriate sentencing range for section 24A deception following R v Kolawole
Application of section 31 defence to delayed false-name asylum applications

notes: Case stated appeal on intoximeter EC/IR software presumption and magistrates' case-management discretion; Divisional Court upheld conviction.

enrichment.short_title: Skinner v DPP: intoximeter software presumption and joint hearing procedure

statutes_considered.title: Magistrates' Courts (Advance Notice of Expert Evidence) Rules 1997

key_facts: Appellant convicted of excess alcohol after two 72 microgram breath readings on a Staines Intoximeter EC/IR device.
Her case was heard together with two others challenging the same machine but not as co-defendants.
District Judge Marshall presumed approved software version 5.23 absent evidence to the contrary.
Appellant was refused cross-examination of another defendant's expert and exclusion of duplicate expert evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Staines Magistrates' Court to the Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; presumption of correct type-approved software held within reasonable limits and trial conduct was a proper exercise of discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Where an approved EC/IR device is shown to be compliant and properly serviced, magistrates may infer it runs the approved software absent evidential challenge; separate cases may be heard together for common expert evidence without full co-accused status.
legal_issues: Whether prosecution could rely on presumption of correct type-approved software
Whether separate 'heard together' procedure was lawful
Limits on cross-examining another defendant's expert witness
Whether continuing a part-heard trial over months was Wednesbury unreasonable

notes: Neighbour dispute over stable title from 1988 deeds of gift; Chadwick LJ allowed appeal and held stable passed to Douglas Turner.

enrichment.short_title: Turner v Wakefield: construction of deeds of gift and stable title
key_facts: Neighbours disputed ownership of a stable in Ab Kettleby following family gifts of cottages and outbuildings in 1988-1993.
Conveyancing plans based on a 1967 OS map wrongly split the brick barn through the stable.
Judge Bray rectified yard titles but held the Wakefields owned the stable and dismissed easement claims.
Appeal was limited to title to the stable under the first and second 1988 conveyances read together.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal from Leicester County Court on permission limited to title to the stable.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declaration that the ground-floor stable and relevant first-floor part were conveyed to Douglas Turner and should form part of title LT332245.
enrichment.ratio: Read together, the 1988 deeds intended the southern ground-floor stable and overlying first-floor area south of the partition to pass to the son; a boundary through the barn aligned with the stable's north wall, not the workshop wall extension on the plan.
legal_issues: Construction of simultaneous deeds of gift using identification-only plans
Whether the stable passed under the first or second 1988 conveyance
Effect of discrepancies between conveyancing plans and buildings on the ground
Whether a flying freehold overhang arose on the first floor

notes: Renewed permission application refused in BBC Resources sex discrimination case; tribunal comparator findings held sufficient despite brevity.

enrichment.short_title: Hillman v BBC Resources: permission to appeal on comparator findings
key_facts: Camera operator Miss Hillman claimed direct sex discrimination and victimisation in work allocation by male 'super supervisors'.

Originating application had not identified actual or hypothetical comparators.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed oral application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal from EAT refusal of permission.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; no real prospect of showing error of law in comparator or burden-of-proof analysis.
enrichment.ratio: Brief but clear tribunal conclusions on diverse actual comparators can suffice; absence of detailed comparator findings is not necessarily an error of law warranting a full rehearing.

notes: Confiscation appeal on tobacco smuggled at Hull; benefit accrued at importation excise duty point per R v Smith (David).

enrichment.short_title: Edwards v R: confiscation after tobacco seized within Hull port

statutes_considered.title: Excise Goods (Holding, Movement, Warehousing and REDS) Regulations 1992

key_facts: Appellant pleaded guilty to fraudulent evasion of duty on 3158 kg of concealed rolling tobacco at Hull.
Tobacco was seized within the port before he left; confiscation order was for £30,257.52, his realisable assets.
He argued no benefit arose because duty had not been evaded until exit from the port enclosure.
Customs undertook not to pursue civil recovery of duty after confiscation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeal against confiscation order following guilty plea.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; pecuniary advantage and benefit obtained at importation when duty became payable.
enrichment.ratio: Excise duty on imported tobacco becomes payable at the finite excise duty point of importation; fraudulent evasion at that moment yields a confiscation benefit regardless of later seizure inside the port, following R v Smith (David).
legal_issues: When importation and the excise duty point occur for intra-port tobacco
Whether evasion requires physical removal from the port area
Whether benefit under section 71 CJA arises before goods leave customs control
Risk of double recovery of duty via confiscation and civil proceedings

notes: Rent Act possession appeal on CPR 6.5(6) service; Brooke LJ held regular default judgment and no arguable defence to suitable alternative accommodation.

enrichment.short_title: Akram v Adam: service at usual residence and setting aside default judgment
key_facts: Protected tenant Mr Adam did not receive possession proceedings posted to 5 Moulsham Drive, his usual residence.
Default possession order was made in September 2003; he applied to set aside judgment in October 2003.
District judge set aside judgment for defective service given long postal difficulties; circuit judge reversed.
Landlord offered suitable alternative accommodation after conversion works approved in earlier proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal from Southend County Court on second appeal from setting aside default possession judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; CPR 6.5(6) service at usual residence was good service and discretion to set aside was properly exercised against a tenant with no real prospect of defence.
enrichment.ratio: Where CPR 6.5(6) conditions are met, posting to usual or last known residence is good service even if not received; a defendant with no arguable defence is not entitled under Article 6 to set aside a regular default judgment as of right.

Whether tenant had real prospect of defending suitable alternative accommodation claim

notes: Leasehold enfranchisement valuation under section 9(1A)(d); development potential included in unimproved comparator per Shalson.

enrichment.short_title: Fattal v John Lyon School: tenant improvements and enfranchisement price
key_facts: Tenants sought to enfranchise a substantially extended Hamilton Terrace house under long leases expiring in 2007.
Major extensions including a swimming pool increased internal area from about 3,834 to over 7,000 square feet.
Lands Tribunal reduced price by deducting tenant improvement value but included development potential in the unimproved valuation.
House of Lords in Shalson had recently held reconversion works were 'improvements' within assumption (d).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal from Lands Tribunal decision on leasehold enfranchisement price.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; diminution under section 9(1A)(d) measured against unimproved value including potential for improvement.
enrichment.ratio: Assumption (d) requires comparing improved value with what the property would have been worth unimproved at the valuation date, including any development potential market participants would pay for; valuation method is for valuers unless statute dictates otherwise.

enrichment.short_title: Westoak v Waltham Forest: proof of debt assignment to asylum invoices
key_facts: Station Estates assigned about £560,592 of bed-and-breakfast asylum debts to Westoak by deed dated 10 October 2001.
Four invoice appendices scheduled the debts; notice was given to Waltham Forest in March-April 2002.
Earlier proceedings settled appendices 3-4 invoices; second claim pursued unpaid appendices 1-2 balances.
Trial judge dismissed for failure to prove assignment after adjournment for proof on borough's late application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal from Leicester County Court judgment dismissing debt claim for want of proved assignment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; assignment to appendices 1-4 proved and case remitted for trial on merits of outstanding invoices.
enrichment.ratio: Unchallenged evidence that a deed was executed with four scheduling appendices and acknowledged notice, together with partial payments under the assignment, suffices to prove the assignment despite confusion in earlier related proceedings.

notes: Permission to appeal refused against refusal of JR over BPP Law School concession and independent reviewer decisions; out of time and no arguable case.

enrichment.short_title: Saiadi v BPP Law School: permission to appeal on concession refusal
key_facts: Mrs Saiadi failed two Bar Vocational Course assessments and her late concession applications were rejected by the BPP Assessment Board and on appeal.
Independent reviewer Gerald Godfrey QC held the school had followed its procedures and its decisions were not manifestly unreasonable.
Judicial review was not brought until August 2003, well outside the three-month CPR time limit.
Sullivan J refused permission and an extension of time; the applicant appeared in person on the permission application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal oral application for permission to appeal against refusal of permission to apply for judicial review and refusal of extension of time.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused on grounds of delay, lack of arguable merit, and no basis to interfere with refusal of adjournment.
enrichment.ratio: Late concession applications under tightly drawn vocational assessment regulations are matters of judgment for the institution; judicial review will not reargue merits, and unexplained delay outside the three-month limit will normally defeat an extension unless strong reasons exist.

Whether the judge erred in refusing an adjournment

notes: Interpleader over frozen Nigerian correspondent accounts; proprietary tracing claims admitted and fund distributed pari passu, rejecting Clayton's Case.

enrichment.short_title: Commerzbank v IMB Morgan: interpleader over 419 fraud correspondent accounts
key_facts: Commerzbank London froze correspondent dollar and sterling accounts of Nigerian stockbroker IMB Morgan after police linked receipts to advance-fee (419) fraud.
Commerzbank brought interpleader proceedings identifying over 100 potential claimants worldwide who had paid into the mingled accounts.
Lawrence Collins J admitted many proprietary tracing and Quistclose-type claims but rejected others for insufficient evidence.
Valid claims far exceeded the balances; the rule in Clayton's Case was displaced and funds were ordered distributed rateably (about 46% sterling, 9% dollar).
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court interpleader application under RSC Order 17 following freezing of correspondent bank accounts and service on international claimants.
enrichment.outcome: Funds paid into court distributed pari passu among admitted claimants in proportion to validated claims; Clayton's Case held inapplicable.
enrichment.ratio: Victims of fraud may trace into mingled correspondent bank accounts; where valid tracing claims exceed the fund and withdrawals cannot practicably be attributed, rateable pari passu distribution is fair and the rule in Clayton's Case should not apply.
legal_issues: Whether claimants had proprietary tracing claims into mingled correspondent accounts
Whether mistaken or Quistclose payments gave rise to trust claims
Whether the rule in Clayton's Case applied to competing innocent beneficiaries
Method of interpleader service on overseas claimants
